zh: 第三、釋四無色定。四無色定者：一、空處；二、識處；三、無所有處；四、非有想非無想處。今釋此四定為二意：一、總釋；二、別釋。一、總釋者，前四禪、四無量定悉依色法故有，今此四定悉依無色法，從境得名，故云無色定。是故經云：「四空滅色道，心心互相依，亦名四空定。」無形無質即是義同虛空，故名四空定，亦名四空定處。此四種定心，亦名定處。此四種定心，以所觀之境為處，如念處、勝處、一切處，悉從所觀處得名。四空定次第之相，在下當明。而不名禪者，前已受名，不應重立，今應更立勝名。復次，此四無色自體支林有闕，不得名禪。
en: Third, explaining the four formless concentrations. The four formless concentrations are: the sphere of boundless space; the sphere of boundless consciousness; the sphere of nothingness; and the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. Here, these four concentrations are explained in two parts: a general explanation; and a particular explanation.

First, the general explanation: the previous four dhyānas and the four immeasurable-mind concentrations are all present in dependence on form-dharma; these present four concentrations, however, are all present in dependence on formless dharma, taking their very name from their own object — hence they are called the formless concentrations. Hence the sūtra says: "The four emptinesses extinguish the path of form, mind after mind mutually depending on one another" — also called the four concentrations of emptiness. Having no shape and no substance, their meaning is the same as empty space itself — hence they are named the four concentrations of emptiness, also called the four spheres of the concentration of emptiness.

These four kinds of concentrated mind are also named "spheres," since these four kinds of concentrated mind take the very object contemplated as their own sphere — just as the foundations of mindfulness, the stations of mastery, and the totality-bases all likewise take their name from the object contemplated. The mark of the four concentrations of emptiness' own sequence will be clarified below. As for why they are not named "dhyāna": having already received their own name earlier, it would not be proper to establish this same name again, and so a more excellent name is established here instead. Furthermore: these four formless attainments are themselves deficient in the substance of a grove-of-factors, and so cannot be named "dhyāna."

zh: 問曰：《纓絡經》說：「五支為因，默然為定體。」此復云何？答曰：此但約義方便立支，非如四禪具足成就支林之法，故諸經論中並不說有支也。
en: Question: the Yingluo Sūtra says: "The five factors serve as the cause, and silence serves as the substance of concentration" — how, then, does this apply here? Answer: this is simply establishing factors as a matter of convenient sense, not the same as the four dhyānas' own complete accomplishment of the dharma of a grove-of-factors — hence the various sūtras and treatises, in general, do not speak of factors being present here at all.

items.en: The Sphere of Boundless Space: Name and Cultivation

zh: 第二、別釋空處，即開為三：一、釋名；二、修行；三、證相。第一、釋名，所以名空處定者，此定最初離三種色，心緣虛空，既與無色相應，故名虛空定。今此空處及上三無色定並是無覺、無觀、聖默然及捨俱所攝，故《摩訶衍》云：「得虛空處定，不苦不樂，其心轉增。」問曰：若虛空無色名空定者，上來諸禪亦見空想，何故不名虛空定耶？答曰：不爾。彼六地中，但是入定心細，不見麁色之相，意謂為空，而實未能觀色，破散色法，斷色繫縛。所以定中或時見色，或不見色，非如空定一向永絕色相。是故六地定中雖有空相，不名虛空無色定也。
en: Second, explaining the sphere of boundless space in particular: this opens into three parts — explaining the name; cultivation; and the mark of realization.

First, explaining the name: as for why it is named the concentration of the sphere of space, this concentration is the very first to leave the three kinds of form behind, the mind taking empty space as its object, corresponding, at this point, with formlessness itself — hence it is named the concentration of empty space. This sphere of space, together with the three formless attainments above it, all belong to the samādhi without initial thought or sustained reflection, noble silence, joined with equanimity — hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: "Having attained the concentration of the sphere of space, free of both suffering and happiness, the mind grows ever further."

Question: if it is empty space's own formlessness that gives the concentration of emptiness its name, then the dhyānas already discussed above also involve a perception of emptiness — why, then, are they not named the concentration of empty space as well? Answer: this does not follow. Within those six stages, it is simply that, upon entering concentration, the mind grows fine, no longer perceiving the mark of coarse form, and so is taken, in one's own mind, to be "empty" — but, in truth, one has not yet actually been able to contemplate form directly, break it apart, and sever the bondage of form. Hence, within those concentrations, form is at times seen and at times not seen — unlike the concentration of emptiness, which leaves the mark of form behind entirely and permanently. Hence, although those six stages of concentration do involve a mark resembling emptiness, they are not named the concentration of empty, formless space.

zh: 第二、明修空方法。就中有二：一、明所修之境；二、明能修之心。一、明所修之境中有二種：一者、障境；二者、相成境。一、障者，行者欲入空處，要須滅三種色：一、可見有對色；二、不可見有對色；三、不可見無對色。故經中說：「過一切色相，滅有對相，不念種種相，入無邊虛空處。」《摩訶衍》云：「過一切色相，即破可見有對色；滅有對相，即是破不可見有對色；不念種種相，是滅不可見無對色。」一切色法不過十一，謂五塵、五根及一入少分，即是色法塵。如《阿毘曇》說：「一則見十，則說有對。」一入少分，是不可見無對，行者欲入虛空處定，必須破此三色，此三種色即是障境。二、成定境者，虛空為智所緣，因此入定，即是成定之境。
en: Second, clarifying the method for cultivating the sphere of space. Within this, there are two parts: clarifying the object to be cultivated; and clarifying the mind that does the cultivating.

First, clarifying the object to be cultivated: this itself is of two kinds — the object that obstructs; and the object that accomplishes concentration. First, as for the obstructing object: the practitioner wishing to enter the sphere of space must extinguish three kinds of form: visible form with resistance; invisible form with resistance; and invisible form without resistance. Hence the sūtra says: "Passing beyond every mark of form, extinguishing the mark of resistance, no longer taking up any of the various marks, one enters the sphere of boundless space." The Mahāyāna treatise says: "'Passing beyond every mark of form' means breaking through visible form with resistance; 'extinguishing the mark of resistance' means breaking through invisible form with resistance; and 'no longer taking up any of the various marks' means extinguishing invisible form without resistance." Every form-dharma whatsoever numbers no more than eleven: the five sense-objects, the five sense-faculties, and a small portion of the sense-base of dharma, this last being itself a form-dharma-object. As the Abhidharma says: "One of them is visible; ten are said to have resistance." The small portion of the dharma-sense-base is invisible and without resistance. The practitioner wishing to enter the concentration of the sphere of space must break through these three kinds of form — these three kinds of form are precisely the obstructing object. Second, as for the object that accomplishes concentration: empty space, taken as the object of wisdom, is the very means by which concentration is entered — this is precisely the object that accomplishes concentration.

zh: 第二、明能修之心，即為二：一、訶讚；二、觀析修習。言訶讚者，如行者欲求虛空處定，應深思色法過罪，所謂若有身色，則內有饑渴、疾病、大小便利、滓穢、麁重弊惡、欺誑虛假等一切諸苦，外受寒熱、刀杖、枷鎖、刑罰等一切諸苦。從先世因緣和合，報得此身，即是種種眾苦之本，不可保著。復次，一切色法繫縛於心，不得自在，即是心之牢獄，令心受惱，無可貪樂。是則略說訶色過罪之相。讚者，讚歎虛空無色，則無此過，虛豁安樂，此處寂靜，無眾惱患。今明訶責、讚歎者，即是修習六行之相。類前可知也。
en: Second, clarifying the mind that does the cultivating: this itself has two parts — reproach and praise; and analytic contemplation.

As for reproach and praise: the practitioner wishing to seek the concentration of the sphere of space should deeply reflect on the faults and offenses of the dharma of form — namely, that, wherever there is a bodily form, there is, within it, hunger, thirst, illness, urination and defecation, filth and impurity, coarse heaviness and repugnance, deception and falsity, every such suffering; and, from outside, it undergoes cold, heat, weapons and rods, fetters and chains, punishment, every such suffering as well. Obtained as a karmic result through the coming together of causes and conditions from past lives, this very body is the root of every manner of suffering, and cannot be relied upon or clung to. Furthermore: every form-dharma whatsoever binds the mind, denying it freedom — it is itself the very prison of the mind, causing the mind to suffer affliction, with nothing in it worth craving or delighting in. This, in brief, describes the mark of reproaching form's own faults and offenses. As for praise: one praises empty, formless space as free of these very faults, vast, open, and at peace — this stage being still and tranquil, free of every affliction and trouble. What is clarified here, reproach and praise, is precisely the mark of cultivating the six practices, understood by the same pattern as before.

zh: 二、明觀析修習。行者於四禪中應作是念：「我今此定，依欲界身具足色法，何故不見？」作此念已，即當一心諦觀己身一切毛道及與九孔，身內空種皆悉虛疎，猶如羅縠，內外相通；亦如芭蕉，重重無實。作是觀時，即便得見。既得見已，復更諦心觀察，見身如簁、如甑、如蜘蛛網，漸漸微末，身分皆盡，不見於身及五根等。如內身既盡，外色亦然。所以者何？內身四微、四大一切色法，不異外身四微、四大一切色法故。
en: Second, clarifying analytic contemplation. The practitioner, within the fourth dhyāna, should reflect: "My present concentration relies upon a body of the desire realm, complete with form-dharma — why, then, do I not see it directly?" Having reflected in this way, one should single-mindedly and closely contemplate every pore and the nine bodily orifices of one's own body, the space-element within the body entirely empty and porous throughout, just like a fine silk gauze, inward and outward freely interpenetrating; and also like a plantain trunk, layer upon layer with nothing solid at its core. Contemplating in this way, one comes to see this directly. Having seen it, one should further and more closely observe, seeing the body as though it were a sieve, a steaming-basket, or a spider's web, growing gradually more and more insubstantial, the bodily parts entirely exhausted, until neither the body nor the five faculties are seen at all. Just as the inward body is thus exhausted, so too is outward form. Why is this? Because the inward body's own four subtle elements and four great elements, every form-dharma present, are no different at all from the outward body's own four subtle elements and four great elements, every form-dharma present there as well.

zh: 復次，行者如是觀時，眼見色壞，故名過色。耳聲、鼻香、舌味、身觸覺壞，故名滅有對相。於二種餘色及無教色種種不分別，故名不念種種別異相。一切色法既滅，但一心緣空，念空不捨，即色定便謝，而空定未發，亦有中間禪。爾時慎勿憂悔，勤加精進，一心念空，當度色難。是則略說修習禪定方法。
en: Furthermore: the practitioner, contemplating in this way, the eye's own seeing of form broken down — this is named "passing beyond form." The ear's sound, the nose's fragrance, the tongue's flavor, and the body's own tactile sensing all broken down as well — this is named "extinguishing the mark of resistance." No longer discriminating among the remaining two kinds of form, nor among the various kinds of unmanifest form (form neither visible nor resistant) — this is named "no longer taking up any of the various distinct marks." Once every form-dharma has thus been extinguished, one simply fixes the mind single-mindedly on emptiness, holding this mindfulness of emptiness without relinquishing it — at this point, the concentration of form passes away and is extinguished, while the concentration of emptiness has not yet arisen; there is, in the interval, an intermediate dhyāna present here as well. At this point, one must take great care not to fall into worry or regret, but instead apply oneself diligently, holding the mind single-mindedly on emptiness, until the difficulty of form is finally overcome. This, in brief, describes the method for cultivating this dhyāna-concentration.

The body-dissolving contemplation here — pores and orifices, then the body as sieve, steaming-basket, and spider's web, until neither the body nor the five faculties are seen at all — extends the treatise's recurring physiological grounding of abstract states (the kalala stage in fascicle 1, the sixteen tactile sensations in fascicle 5) into its most radical instance yet: form is not denied philosophically but watched dissolving experientially, pore by pore, until nothing is left to hold onto. The three-kinds-of-form scheme (visible-with-resistance, invisible-with-resistance, invisible-without-resistance) gives real content to what "passing beyond form" actually requires — not just the coarse visible world but two further, subtler layers most practitioners would never think to name.

quiz.q: Why are the four formless concentrations so named?
options: the dhyānas and immeasurable minds depend on form; these depend on formless dharma and are named from their object
quiz.why: The four dhyānas and immeasurable minds exist in dependence on form; these four depend on formless dharma and take their name from their object.

quiz.q: Why are the four formless attainments not called "dhyāna"? Which two reasons are given?
options: the name was already given earlier, so a more excellent name is used; and they are deficient in a grove of factors
quiz.why: Having already received a name earlier, the same name should not be repeated, so a more excellent one is used; further, they lack a full grove of factors.

quiz.q: The Yingluo Sūtra speaks of five factors as cause. How does the text reconcile this with saying the formless attainments lack factors?
options: the five factors are the hindrances
factors are posited only as a matter of convenient sense, not complete as in the four dhyānas
quiz.why: Factors are established only as a matter of convenient sense, unlike the four dhyānas' complete grove of factors, which is why other texts do not speak of factors here.

quiz.q: The earlier dhyānas also involve a perception of emptiness. Why are they not called the concentration of space?
options: there the mind is merely too fine to perceive coarse form; form has not been broken apart, so it is sometimes seen and sometimes not
the space concentration is in the desire realm
they have no perception of emptiness
quiz.why: In those six stages the mind grows fine and does not perceive coarse form, but form has not actually been broken apart, so it is sometimes seen; the space concentration leaves form behind permanently.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, which kind of form does each phrase of the sūtra break through?
options: passing beyond marks of form: visible with resistance; extinguishing resistance: invisible with resistance; not taking up marks: invisible without resistance
quiz.why: "Passing beyond every mark of form" breaks visible form with resistance; "extinguishing the mark of resistance" breaks invisible form with resistance; "not taking up the various marks" extinguishes invisible form without resistance.

quiz.q: In analytic contemplation for the sphere of space, how is the body seen first and then later?
options: first as porous as silk gauze or a plantain trunk; then as a sieve, steaming-basket, or spider's web, until it disappears
quiz.why: First the body's inner space is seen as porous as silk gauze and hollow as a plantain; then as a sieve, steaming-basket, or spider's web, growing ever finer until the body is no longer seen.
